finding: The entire measured benefit of --role under `tp run` requires a change to the driver that this release never asks for. §4 states that under `tp run` each role unit's brief command is exactly `tp review <spec>` / `tp audit <spec>` (spec/0.35.0.md §3.3.1), and §4.2 prices the win as '41 KB of context to read 10 KB of it; --role removes three quarters of that, per unit, per round'. But §4.1 only adds a flag to the two commands. Nothing in §4, §5 or §6 requires the driver's generated brief command to become `tp review <spec> --role $TP_UNIT_ID`, and no test covers it. An implementer who builds exactly what §4.1 specifies ships a release where the 123,045 wasted bytes per round are still wasted, because nothing under `tp run` passes the flag. The word 'brief' appears once in the whole spec, in the sentence that identifies the cost.
suggestion: Add a normative bullet to §4.1: the driver's per-unit brief command for a review-role/audit-role unit is `tp <review|audit> <spec> --role <unit id>`, naming where that command is constructed and what it does for non-role unit kinds. Add a test to §6: a role unit's brief command as generated by the driver contains `--role` with the unit's own id, and the payload that command produces holds exactly one prompt. Without it, state in §5 that this release ships the flag and spec/0.3x.0 adopts it, and move §4.2's measured claim to that release.

finding: The entire measured saving of the release's only new flag is unreachable as specified, because nothing on any path passes it. §4.3 item 1 establishes from internal/engine/childenv.go that the child environment carries no prompt and that "The unit calls tp review itself"; spec/0.35.0.md §3.3.1 fixes that brief invocation as tp review <spec>, with no --role. So §4.2's claim -- "Under tp run a role unit spends 41 KB of its context to read 10 KB of it; --role removes three quarters of that, per unit, per round" -- describes a saving that requires the driver to rewrite the brief command, or the agent definitions to carry the flag. This spec makes neither change and §5 does not fence either as a Non-Goal. It also cannot be delivered the way §2 and §3 deliver their behaviour, by a prompt clause: the instruction to pass --role would live inside the payload the flag exists to avoid fetching, so the unit must already have paid the 175 KB to read it. §1 says §4's cost "is paid hardest under tp run"; on that path the flag as written saves nothing.
suggestion: Name the caller that passes --role. Either (a) state that the driver's brief command becomes tp review <spec> --role $TP_UNIT_ID and amend spec/0.35.0.md §3.3.1 accordingly, with a test that the emitted brief carries the flag, or (b) have the unit derive it from TP_UNIT_ID via the agent definitions, and say so, or (c) if neither ships here, move the tp run benefit out of §4.2 into a Non-Goal and restate §4 as a human-orchestrator flag only -- which is the only beneficiary the section actually funds.

finding: §4.1 legalises --role in four `tp review` modes but defines the name-matching set only for one of them, and the definition it gives refuses what §6 test 11 requires to succeed. Bullet 2 says `<name>` is matched against 'the active role set for that phase — the same set the unrestricted invocation would emit'; those two halves are the same set only in the default and --diff-from modes. §6 test 4 states that under `--perspective testing` the single emitted prompt carries role `test-planner`, which is not a member of the active role set; `--verify` likewise emits a single non-corpus prompt. So `--role test-planner --perspective testing` is refused with exit 2 by bullet 2 while test 11 requires exit 0 with one prompt, and `--role architect --perspective testing` passes bullet 2's validation but selects zero of the emitted entries — an outcome bullet 1 ('reduced to the single entry whose role equals <name>') does not define. Three of the four legal modes are unbuildable as written.
suggestion: State the matching set per mode: define it as the set of `prompts[].role` values the same invocation would emit with the flag removed (which makes --perspective/--verify self-consistent), and say what the exit-2 hint lists in a mode whose panel is a single pseudo-role. Then either drop --perspective and --verify from the legal column — they already emit one prompt, so the flag buys nothing there — or add the zero-match case to bullet 1 with its exit code.

finding: §1's 'What it costs' prices the two clauses per prompt, on a denominator §4 of the same release exists to prove wrong. It says '375 bytes ... Against this spec's own review prompt of 10,238 bytes that is 3.7%'. Two things are off, and the second is the load-bearing one. (a) The real round-3 role prompt is 19,512 bytes, so the ratio is 1.9%. (b) §4 establishes, and I re-measured, that the clauses are emitted into EVERY prompt of every invocation and that every unit receives the whole panel: 374 bytes x 5 prompts x 4 units = 7,480 bytes per round, twenty times the headline, and that is the figure an operator deciding whether to ship this is entitled to. §1 opens by saying the benefit is not uniform and prices it honestly; it then prices the cost on the one denominator the rest of the document is about dismantling.
suggestion: Give the cost as emitted x panel x units for the default path, and separately for the --role path where it is emitted once. That is two numbers, it is the same measurement §4 already performs, and it makes §1's own 'stated up front because it is not uniform' framing apply to the cost as well as the benefit.

finding: The clause as worded — "Do not modify the working tree. Read anything; write only the output file this prompt names" — forbids the unit from running tp itself, which is the only way to check most of this spec's own claims. Observed first-hand while reviewing this round: `tp review <spec>` rewrote spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/snapshot-round-3.md, and `tp audit <spec>` created spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/snapshot-audit-round-1.md — both plain, read-shaped, prompt-emitting invocations with no --record, no --merge and no write flag, and both left the tree dirty under git. §2.4 removes the escape hatch ("No perturbation recipe is offered") and §2.2's own text is built out of claims that can only be settled by running the binary ("verified on this spec's own round-3 prompt", "output_path is a key both commands emit"), as is every "Verified against the shipped binary" line in §2.1, §4.1 and §4.3. A unit that obeys the clause literally cannot produce the evidence this project's rules demand; a unit that produces the evidence violates the clause. Under `tp run` the §6.3 fence turns this from a wording problem into a hard denial, because the allow-list is one path.
suggestion: Carve out tp's own state directory, or scope the clause to what it means: "Do not modify the source or the spec. Read anything, and run read-only commands including tp itself; write findings only to the output file this prompt names." If the narrow wording is intended, §2.4 must say how a unit is supposed to verify a claim about emitted output, and §6 needs a test that the clause does not forbid the invocation named in the unit's own brief.

finding: §2.2's clause ('Read anything; write only the output file this prompt names') and §2.1's fence analysis both model a write as an agent tool call. The units are told to run tp commands, and tp's own prompt-emitting commands write repository state as a side effect - a channel neither hook in §2.1's table can see, because a PreToolUse hook inspects the tool call, not what a subprocess does after it is allowed. Confirmed by tp's own help text: `tp review --no-state` is documented as 'Disable all review-state reads and writes (pre-0.23.0 manual behavior)', which is a statement that the default writes. Demonstrated in this round, unintentionally: verifying §4's byte figures and §2.3's placement required running `tp review spec/0.36.0.md` and `tp audit spec/0.35.0.md`, and those runs rewrote spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/snapshot-round-3.md and created spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/snapshot-audit-round-1.md - inside a role unit, with the §6.2 fence active, while obeying the clause as written. So the clause is not merely under-enforced on the interactive path (Non-Goal 4's admission); it is unsatisfiable for any unit that verifies a claim about tp's own emission, which is most of what a reviewer of THIS spec must do, and §2.1's 'Denies a source write?' column overstates what the §6.3 fence buys because it does not cover subprocess writes at all.
suggestion: Name the channel. Extend the clause, or a sentence beside it in §2.2, to cover it - e.g. 'if you run tp to check a claim, pass --no-state' - and add a row or a footnote to §2.1's table recording that neither hook constrains what a permitted subprocess writes, so the §6.3 fence bounds tool writes only. If --no-state is the answer, say so in §2.4 alongside the perturbation discussion, since a reviewer of a spec about the emitted prompt has to run the emitter to review it.

finding: Nothing in §2 or §3 states the condition under which the clauses are emitted; the only statement of it is a test's negative. §2.3's rule is unconditional — 'Both clauses are appended to the existing `## Unit framing` section, after its last existing line' — and §1 says they 'go into every emitted role prompt'. §6 test 4 then requires them absent from `--perspective testing|documentation|code-audit` prompts. The prompts §2.3 describes and the prompts test 4 exempts are distinguished by something the spec never names: the test offers 'role test-planner and an empty output_path' as a description, not as a predicate. An implementer must guess between at least three inequivalent rules — emit when `output_path` is non-empty, emit when the role is a member of the active role set, or emit only in the default/--diff-from modes — and they differ on exactly the cases §4.1 has just legalised.
suggestion: Put the predicate in §2.3 as normative text, in the same terms the emitter can evaluate ('the clauses are emitted for a prompt whose `output_path` is non-empty, and for no other prompt'), and have test 4 assert the predicate rather than three examples of it. State whether a prompt with an empty `output_path` still carries a `## Unit framing` section at all, since §2.2's antecedent argument depends on that section naming a file.

finding: The exact bytes that join the clauses to the prompt are left to the implementer while §6 makes them load-bearing. §2.3 fixes the order and 'one blank line between them' but never states the separator between the section's last existing line and §2's clause — one LF or two. §2.2 compounds it by calling a single-line string 'LF-separated, with no leading or trailing blank line', which is either vacuous or an instruction to append a trailing LF; 'no trailing blank line' does not decide whether there is a trailing newline. Test 5 asserts the byte-count difference 'is exactly the two clauses plus their separators' and test 3 asserts offsets, so both tests have a different expected value for each of the four legal readings, and the implementer cannot write either test without inventing the answer. The anchor is also mobile: the section's last line varies with the file-reading situation, so 'after its last existing line' resolves to different text in different prompts.
suggestion:
Give the appended block as one literal in §2.3, exactly as it is concatenated — e.g. `
` + clause2 + `

` + clause3 + `
` — and state the total added byte count there so test 5 has a number to assert rather than a phrase to interpret. Drop 'LF-separated' from §2.2, since the string contains no separator.

finding: The two rules that fix the emitted bytes contradict each other for §3's clause. §2.2 emits its string "with no leading or trailing blank line", and §3.2 emits its string "on the terms §2.2 and §2.3 fix" — so §2.2 forbids a leading blank line on §3's clause while §2.3 mandates "one blank line between them". Two engineers write byte-equality assertions over different strings. The separator before §2's clause is unspecified for the same reason: §2.3 says "after its last existing line" and §2.2 forbids a leading blank line, which on the shipped audit prompt (verified: tp audit's Unit framing section ends with an indented "  - <path>" bullet list) glues the clause onto the file list as if it were another path entry. Test 5 depends on the answer — it asserts "exactly the two clauses plus their separators" as a byte count, and the separator byte count is not derivable from the spec.
suggestion: Specify the appended region as one literal block rather than as two strings plus a placement rule: give the exact bytes appended to the section, including the newline(s) before §2's clause and the newline(s) between the two clauses. Either drop §2.2's "no leading or trailing blank line" or scope it explicitly to the clause string itself, not to its separators. Then state test 5's expected delta as an explicit integer.

finding: §2.3 pins the clauses' position relative to the literal header `## Unit framing`, and tp embeds changed spec sections verbatim into the prompt body - so on this spec the anchor is not unique. Verified on the round-3 architect prompt (clean env): the string `## Unit framing` occurs three times, at offsets 17734, 18319 and 18744, and only the last is the real section; the first two come from §2.2's and §2.3's own quotation of the header inside the embedded 'Changed sections since round 2' block. The regression prompt has the same three occurrences (5905, 6490, 88566) and 41 occurrences of 'Unit framing'. §6 test 3 requires the clauses to 'fall inside the `## Unit framing` section ... asserted on offsets, not on presence'. An offset assertion written against the first match of that header is wrong on exactly this spec and silently right on every spec that never quotes it, so the test passes on the corpus that does not exercise the hazard and fails on the one that does. This is the same self-reference the release has to live with generally: a spec whose subject is the emitted prompt puts its own fixture strings into the prompt.
suggestion: Anchor placement on something the emitted body cannot contain rather than on a quoted header: specify the clauses as appended to the LAST occurrence of the `## Unit framing` header in the emitted prompt, or better, have the emitter append them at the point it constructs that section and have §6 test 3 assert their offsets relative to the output-file line of the final section (last index, not first). State the rule in §2.3 so an implementer does not reach for `strings.Index`.

finding: §3.1, §3.3 and Non-Goal 5 all route this release's central unclosed hole to `spec/0.41.0.md` §2 - '§3.1 and §3.3 explain why the predicate is unchanged and leave it to spec/0.41.0.md §2', 'Whether a partial file should ever complete a unit is spec/0.41.0.md §2's question'. That section does not contain the question. spec/0.41.0.md §2 is 'Sharding a role's checklist': it specifies the split key, says shards are 'merged as today', and states as its invariant that 'the merged result of N shards is the same set of rows a single unit would have produced; no item is dropped at a boundary; no item is judged twice.' That invariant PRESUPPOSES every shard completes; it never asks whether an incomplete unit may count as complete. The 0.41.0 section that reasons about a narrowed round hiding a verdict is §3 (Incremental rounds), and its disposition is the opposite one - such a round is 'uncounted for convergence' unless the skip predicate is derived from something tp can see. So the escape hatch for §3.3's own admission that this release 'makes that misreading easier' points at a section that will not answer it, and 0.41.0 is sixth of seven in the queue behind 0.40.0's measurement.
suggestion: Re-target the deferral. Either cite spec/0.41.0.md §3, whose 'uncounted unless the skip predicate is checkable' rule is the shape of the answer, or - better, since the hole is this release's to widen - state the interim rule here: a .part file is never promoted and never merged as a complete unit, and a role whose file is missing from a round is named in the recorded round rather than merging clean. If neither is in scope, say plainly that the hole stays open and name the release that closes it, rather than pointing at a section that does not hold the question.

finding: Every figure in §4 and §4.2 is roughly 4.3x low against the round it names as its source. §4 says 'Measured on this spec's own round 3, four roles: One role's prompt 10,183 - 10,334 | One invocation's payload 41,015 | Four units, one round 164,060 -- of which 123,045 is never read.' Re-measured on round 3's actual emission: role prompts are 19,359-19,512 bytes, one invocation is 174,827 bytes, four units are ~699,308 of which ~621,585 is never read. §4.2's derived ratio is wrong in the same direction: a unit spends 175 KB to read 19.5 KB, so --role removes ~89%, not 'three quarters'. The cause is structural rather than arithmetic and it is the AX point: the emitted prompt embeds the unresolved-findings preamble, which grows monotonically with every recorded round, so any byte table stated as a fixed fact is stale the round after it is written -- this one was already stale in the round it claims to measure.
suggestion: State the measurement with the inputs that make it reproducible (round number, role count, whether regression is included) and give it as a ratio plus one dated absolute, not as a table of absolutes presented as constants. Better: derive the claim from the invariant instead -- 'a unit reads 1/N of what it is sent, and the payload grows with recorded findings' -- which stays true as the numbers move, and let §6 test 5 own the exact bytes.

finding: §4's byte table omits the single largest prompt in the payload, and --role as defined cannot select it. Re-measured on the exact emission §4 cites -- this spec's own round 3 -- the unrestricted `tp review spec/0.36.0.md` payload contains FIVE prompts[] entries, not four: architect 19414, ax-economist 19512, implementer 19438, tester 19359, and `regression` 89397 bytes. The regression entry is 53% of the 167120 prompt bytes and larger than all four role prompts combined (77723). It is not a table row, not a corpus role (.tp/reviewers/ holds exactly the four; skipped_roles is []), and it is not covered by §4.1's selector: '<name> is matched against the active role set for that phase -- the same set the unrestricted invocation would emit' names two sets that differ by exactly this entry. On the narrow reading `--role regression` exits 2 and the flag leaves the majority of the payload in place; on the wide reading the hint 'listing the active roles' lists a set that does not include the accepted name. Either way the section's economics are computed over a panel that is missing its biggest item.
suggestion: Decide which set --role ranges over and say it once, in one sentence, rather than by two phrases that disagree. If regression (and any other non-corpus prompt the command emits) is selectable, add it to §4's table with its measured bytes and to the hint; if it is not, say so explicitly and re-derive §4.2's saving over the payload that actually ships, since regression alone is more than half of it.

finding: §4's panel model counts four roles and its arithmetic does not reproduce against the round it names. Measured just now on this spec's own round 3 with the freshly built binary and no TP_* environment: `tp review spec/0.36.0.md` emits FIVE prompts[] entries - architect, ax-economist, implementer, tester and regression - a payload of 175,410 bytes, the four corpus prompts at 19,016-19,167 bytes each, and the regression prompt at 88,894 bytes, i.e. 51% of the payload on its own. §4's table states 'One role's prompt 10,183 - 10,334', 'One invocation's payload 41,015' and 'Four units, one round 164,060'; §1 restates the same per-prompt figure as 10,238 bytes and derives its 3.7% from it. The arithmetic error is secondary to the modelling error: the fifth entry is a prompts[] object with role='regression' and a non-empty output_path, tp's own emitted review_loop.instruction tells the orchestrator to 'Process the regression prompt first', and §4.1 gives no ruling on whether `--role regression` is matched or refused. The mechanism is specified against a panel that is not the panel the command emits, and the entry it omits is the largest one and the first one an orchestrator asks for.
suggestion: Re-measure §4's table against `tp review spec/0.36.0.md` as of the round the spec cites, and print the command used so the figures are reproducible. Then state explicitly whether the regression entry is inside or outside the set --role selects from: if inside, add it to §4.1's matching set and to §6 test 6's coverage; if outside, say so and say what `--role regression` does. Recompute §1's percentage from the corrected per-prompt size.

finding: §4's table is labelled "Measured on this spec's own round 3, four roles" and none of its three numbers reproduces on round 3 of this spec. Verified with the current binary on the current tree: the unrestricted invocation emits five prompts, not four (architect, ax-economist, implementer, tester, regression); one role's prompt is 19,284–19,437 bytes, not 10,183–10,334; one invocation's payload is 173,842 bytes, not 41,015. The cause is that the payload embeds the previous-findings list, which grows every recorded round — a state dependence test 12 explicitly recognises ("a committed blob would encode this repository's review state on the day it was written") while §4 presents the same quantity as a fixed fact. §4.2 inherits the error: on the measured numbers a unit reads 19.3 KB of 173.8 KB, so --role removes about 89%, not "three quarters".
suggestion: State the numbers with the conditions that make them reproducible (which round, which corpus, whether the regression entry is counted, which tp version emitted them) or give them as a ratio derived from the panel size — one prompt of N — rather than as byte counts. Correct "four roles" to the panel the command actually emits, and restate §4.2's fraction as (N-1)/N so it cannot go stale between rounds.

finding: --role is a second prompt-selector on the same axis as the --perspective flag that already ships, and §4 never compares them. §4.3 spends four numbered items retiring --out-dir, but the alternative that is actually adjacent is never raised: `--perspective regression` already reduces prompts[] to exactly one entry -- which is --role's whole contract -- and this repository's own review_loop instruction recommends running it that way ('you may run tp review <spec> --perspective regression alone as an uncounted delta pass'). §4.1 then makes the two composable ('--role is legal in ... --perspective'), and §6 test 11 asserts of that combination only that it 'exits 0 and emits one prompt' -- a condition --perspective alone already satisfies, so no test in the release can show --role did anything when the two are combined. Adding a knob whose behaviour in a documented combination is indistinguishable from the knob that was already there is surface the spec has not earned.
suggestion:
Add a subsection to §4.3 that treats --perspective as the rejected alternative it is: either --role widens the existing selector (one knob, one code path, --perspective

and --role as two spellings of the same filter) or the two compose, in which case §4.1 must say what `--role tester --perspective testing` emits, given that the perspective's single prompt carries role test-planner and is not in the active role set. Then give test 11 a discriminating assertion -- the emitted role, not the count.

finding: §4.1 bullet 2 fixes the matching set ("<name> is matched against the active role set for that phase - the same set the unrestricted invocation would emit") and the §4.1 table declares --role legal in --perspective and --verify. Those two clauses cannot both hold: verified on the shipped binary, `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --verify --findings <f>` emits exactly one prompts[] entry with role 'verifier' (category 'verification', empty output_path), and `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --perspective regression` emits one entry with role 'regression'. Neither name is in the active review role set (.tp/reviewers/ = architect, ax-economist, implementer, tester), so bullet 2 refuses every name those modes can produce with exit 2, while §6 test 11 requires `--role` with --perspective and with --verify to exit 0 and emit one prompt. The appositive in bullet 2 is the root error: 'the active role set for that phase' and 'the same set the unrestricted invocation would emit' are the same set only in the default and --diff-from modes, and §6 test 4 says so itself when it records that --perspective testing's single prompt carries role 'test-planner'.
suggestion: Decide the semantics rather than asserting the two sets are one. Either (a) restrict the 'legal in' column to the modes that emit the corpus panel - default and --diff-from - and add --perspective and --verify to the refused column with exit 2 (single-prompt mode, nothing to select), or (b) redefine the matching set per invocation as 'the set of prompts[].role values this same invocation would emit unrestricted', drop the 'active role set' phrasing, and say explicitly that under --perspective/--verify the only legal value is the one role that mode produces. Then rewrite test 11 to name the concrete legal value per mode (--role verifier with --verify, --role regression with --perspective regression) instead of asserting exit 0 for an unnamed name.

finding: §4.1's 'Every other top-level key is unchanged' freezes a key whose content becomes false under the flag, and §6 test 7 pins the mistake byte-for-byte. The emitted payload carries `review_loop.instruction`, which on this very round reads 'For each prompt, spawn a sub-agent via the Agent tool ... Process the regression prompt first and apply its findings before or together with the three role prompts.' A `--role implementer` payload holds one prompt and no regression prompt, so the instruction directs its reader to spawn agents for prompts that are not there and to sequence against a prompt the payload omits. The implementer is given a rule ('unchanged') that forbids the obvious fix, and a test that fails if the fix is applied, with no statement anywhere that the mismatch was considered.
suggestion: Either exempt `review_loop.instruction` from the byte-identity rule and say what it becomes under --role (one sentence naming the single role and dropping the panel-ordering clause), or state in §4.1 that the instruction is deliberately panel-scoped and that a --role caller must ignore it — and have test 7 assert the exemption rather than the identity.

finding: Test 11 cannot fail for the reason it exists. It asserts that --role with --perspective, with --diff-from and with --verify "exits 0 and emits one prompt". Verified on the shipped binary: `tp review <spec> --verify --findings <f>` already emits exactly one prompt (role "verifier", output_path "") and `tp review <spec> --perspective regression` already emits exactly one prompt (role "regression"). Both modes satisfy the assertion before --role exists. An implementation that parses --role and then ignores it entirely in these modes passes test 11 unchanged. The test also never names the role value it passes, which is the only input that could make it discriminating.
suggestion: Name the role argument and assert both directions per mode: --role <the role that mode emits> exits 0 and yields that prompt, and --role <any other name> exits 2. If --role is intended to be a no-op in a mode that already emits exactly one prompt, say so in §4.1 and delete that leg of the test rather than asserting a tautology.

finding: Tests 4 and 12 decide the same prompt in opposite directions. Test 4 defines the non-role prompt by enumeration (--perspective testing with role test-planner and an empty output_path, plus documentation and code-audit) and claims this pins the rule "for every non-role prompt rather than for one". Verified against the shipped binary: there is a fourth perspective, --perspective regression, and it is the case the enumeration must decide. Under `tp review <spec> --perspective regression` it emits role "regression" with output_path "" — a non-role prompt by the spec's own discriminator. Under the unrestricted default invocation the same panel carries a "regression" entry with output_path "review-r3-regression.ndjson" — a role prompt by that same discriminator. Test 12 then closes it the other way: the default payload differs from v0.35.2's "only by the two clauses inside each prompts[].prompt", and "each" includes the default panel's regression entry that test 4's rule excludes.
suggestion: Replace the enumeration with a predicate — e.g. a prompt receives both clauses if and only if its output_path is non-empty — and state the consequence for the default panel's regression entry in §2.3. Reword test 4 to assert that predicate over every emitted prompt of both commands in every prompt-emitting mode, and reword test 12 to say "each prompts[].prompt whose output_path is non-empty".

finding: Tests 5 and 12 both compare against a v0.35.2 payload and neither says how the implementer obtains that side of the comparison. Test 5 needs 'the difference between a v0.35.2 role prompt and a v0.36.0 one, for the same spec and corpus'; test 12 needs 'the payload ... differs from v0.35.2's only by the two clauses'. Test 12 then closes all three available routes: it refuses a committed blob explicitly ('generated by the test from the current corpus rather than committed'), and code generated by the test in the v0.36.0 tree produces the v0.36.0 payload, not v0.35.2's. The remaining route — building the v0.35.2 tag and shelling out to that binary from a Go test — is a toolchain dependency the spec never mentions and the quality gate could not run offline. As written, a test that fails on the correct implementation is as easy to write as one that passes.
suggestion: Name the mechanism: assert the invariant that does not need the old side — take the v0.36.0 payload, delete the two clause blocks from every `prompts[].prompt`, and assert the result equals a payload the same test generates with clause emission disabled via a test seam; or state that the v0.35.2 side is a committed golden generated by a documented `go run` at that tag with the state-dependent inputs pinned, and say which inputs are pinned.

finding: §6 test 4 makes 'an empty output_path' the discriminator for a prompt that is 'not a role unit's', and §2.2 grounds the clause's antecedent on the output file the prompt names. Verified on the shipped binary, that discriminator classifies the SAME role two opposite ways depending on invocation: `tp review spec/0.36.0.md` emits role 'regression' with output_path 'review-r3-regression.ndjson', while `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --perspective regression` emits role 'regression' with output_path ''. Both invocations are documented workflow - tp's own review_loop.instruction says the orchestrator 'may run tp review spec/0.36.0.md --perspective regression alone as an uncounted delta pass'. So the same agent, doing the same regression sweep, in the same working tree, receives both isolation and incremental-write clauses when the round emits it and neither when the delta pass emits it. That is precisely the false-finding scenario §2 opens with: a concurrent unit mutating the tree because its prompt did not say not to.
suggestion: Do not derive 'is a role unit' from output_path emptiness. Either fix the emitter so --perspective regression carries the same output_path the default invocation gives it (and say so in §2.3), or state the clause rule on a stable property - e.g. emit both clauses in every prompt that carries a role and a checklist, regardless of output_path, and reword §2.2's clause so it does not depend on the file being named. Then rewrite test 4 to assert against that property, and add the --perspective regression case explicitly, since it is the one the discriminator gets wrong.

finding: §7 is the release gate and it names no procedure, no artifact and no pass criterion. 'Replayed against the recorded rounds in `spec/.tp-review/` and shown not to lose a finding tp used to surface' does not say what is replayed (the recorded rounds are findings NDJSON — they contain no prompts to re-emit), what is run against them, what output the replay produces, who compares it to what, or what result blocks the tag. The two mechanisms have opposite replay shapes and the section treats them as one: §2/§3 add bytes to a prompt, so 'losing a finding' can only be measured by re-running rounds with agents (non-deterministic, and the recorded rounds hold no prompt text), whereas --role's suppression risk is mechanical and checkable by comparing panels. An implementer cannot build, schedule or budget this gate, and cannot tell when it has been satisfied.
suggestion: Split §7 by mechanism and make each half executable. For --role: a deterministic check that the union of `--role <r>` payloads over the active set is byte-identical to the unrestricted payload's `prompts[]` — that is a test, not a gate. For §2/§3: state what artifact the replay produces (e.g. a per-round diff of finding counts and class slugs), name the script or command that produces it, and give the number that blocks the release.

finding: §7 is the release's only gate and it has no pass/fail predicate. "Nothing here ships until §2's and §3's clauses are replayed against the recorded rounds in spec/.tp-review/ and shown not to lose a finding tp used to surface" names no procedure, no list of rounds in scope, no definition of "lose a finding", and no test in §6 backs it. It is also not runnable as described against the mechanism it says it guards: spec/.tp-review/ holds findings NDJSON, not emitted prompts, so replaying a recorded round exercises --record and --merge, neither of which emits a prompt or accepts --role. Two engineers cannot agree on whether the gate passed, which for a stated release blocker is the whole cost.
suggestion: State the gate as an experiment with an observable. Name the rounds in scope, name the artifact compared (the emitted prompt per role, before and after), and give the failure condition mechanically — e.g. the v0.36.0 --role <r> prompt is byte-identical to the v0.35.2 panel entry for <r> apart from the clause block, for every role in the corpus. If the real concern is that --role lets an operator drop a role, state that as a check on the invocation rather than on the recorded findings.

finding: §1's cost figure does not reproduce and test 5 has no other source for its number. Measured on the exact strings §2.2 and §3.2 fix: 197 + 177 = 374 bytes, 34 + 35 = 69 words — not "375 bytes, 69 words". The word count matches, so this is an off-by-one in the byte figure rather than a different string; but test 5 is specified as "asserted as a byte count" and §1 is the only place the spec states one, so an implementer writing test 5 from the spec writes a test that fails against a correct implementation. The denominator is stale too: this spec's round-3 tester prompt measures 19,284 bytes, which makes the ratio about 1.9%, not the "3.7%" against "10,238 bytes".
suggestion: Correct the figure to 374 bytes, state the separator bytes separately once §2.3 is unambiguous, and put the expected delta in §6 as an explicit integer so test 5 has one source. Restate the percentage against a named reproducible prompt, or drop it — the argument does not need it.

finding: §2.2 argues that naming 'the output file' rather than 'the findings file' is what makes one string serve both commands, because '`tp audit` produces result rows, not findings'. The antecedent it points at is the framing line, and that line is itself in findings vocabulary — the emitted prompt names the file with 'Write this round's findings to: ...'. So under `tp audit` the sentence the new clause depends on already commits the error the new clause was worded to avoid, and §2 neither notices nor asks for that line to change. An implementer following §5's Non-Goal 6 ('the checklist items, role rules and output schema are untouched') has no authority to reword it and no statement that it should stay.
suggestion: Say explicitly in §2.2 that the existing framing line is out of scope and keeps its wording, or bring it into scope with the same verbatim treatment the two clauses get (one string per command, or one command-neutral string). Either way the release should not leave the antecedent and the clause disagreeing about what the file holds.

finding: §2.2 fixes the antecedent for "the output file this prompt names" by quoting one of two forms the emitter actually produces. It says the prompt "reads `Write this round's findings to: review-r3-architect.ndjson`", verified on this spec's round-3 prompt. That is the interactive form. Verified on the shipped binary with TP_ROUND_DIR and TP_UNIT_ID set — the tp run environment of spec/0.35.0.md §3.3, and the path §4 says pays this release's cost hardest — the same line reads `Write this round's findings to: /…/.tp/rounds/0.36.0/review-r3/role-tester.ndjson.part`: a different basename, a different extension and an absolute path. §2.2 records neither form as normative and test 3 anchors its offsets on "the line naming the output file" without saying which environment the test runs in, so the anchor a test matches on is environment-dependent.
suggestion: State that the antecedent is the line beginning with a fixed prefix (`Write this round's findings to: `) and that placement is asserted relative to that prefix rather than to a full line. Record both emitted forms in §2.2 so an implementer does not pin the test to the interactive one, and add the tp run form to test 3's cases.

finding: §2.2 rests the clause's antecedent on a quoted verification that does not match the artifact, and the real artifact undercuts §2.2's own vocabulary argument. It says the emitted prompt 'ends with a ## Unit framing section that names the file -- verified on this spec's own round-3 prompt, which reads `Write this round's findings to: review-r3-architect.ndjson`'. The actual round-3 prompt reads `Write this round's findings to: /Users/.../.tp/rounds/0.36.0/review-r3/role-architect.ndjson.part` -- absolute, a different naming scheme, and a .part suffix. More consequentially: the line says 'findings', and internal/cli/prompt_framing.go:59 emits that one hardcoded string with no phase branch, so it says 'findings' in tp audit prompts too. §2.2's third paragraph rejects 'the findings file' in the clause precisely because 'tp audit produces result rows, not findings' -- but the antecedent the clause points at is that rejected vocabulary. The clause's command-neutrality is bought by pointing at a sentence that is not command-neutral.
suggestion: Re-quote the framing line as it is actually emitted. Then either accept that 'the output file this prompt names' resolves to a review-worded sentence in audit prompts and say the wording of that sentence is out of scope, or bring the framing line into scope and make it phase-aware -- but do not argue command-neutrality from an antecedent that is not.

finding: §2.2's verification quotes a string the emitter does not produce. It says the antecedent was 'verified on this spec's own round-3 prompt, which reads `Write this round's findings to: review-r3-architect.ndjson`'. The round-3 architect prompt actually reads `Write this round's findings to: /Users/.../.tp/rounds/0.36.0/review-r3/role-architect.ndjson.part` — an absolute path, the `role-<id>` naming scheme, and the `.part` suffix that spec/0.35.0.md §3.3.1 requires. Three of the four things an implementer would take from the quote are wrong. It matters beyond tidiness because §2.3 anchors the clause on this line and test 3 asserts offsets relative to it, so an implementer writing that test from §2.2's quote writes it against a line that does not exist.
suggestion: Replace the quoted string with the emitted one, verbatim and with the path elided as `<TP_ROUND_DIR>/role-<id>.ndjson.part`, and say that the value is the same `output_path` the payload carries so the test can assert against the key rather than against prose.

finding: §2.3 pins the separator BETWEEN the two clauses ('one blank line between them') and says nothing about the separator before the first one, while §2.2 says the clause is emitted 'with no leading or trailing blank line'. Read together they force §2's clause to be glued directly onto whatever the section's last existing line is. Verified on the shipped binary this lands badly for tp audit: `tp audit spec/0.35.0.md`'s role prompt ends its Unit framing section with 'File reading: this prompt names source files but does NOT inline their contents - read these files yourself before judging them:' followed by an indented bullet list ('  - .github/workflows/ci.yml', '  - internal/...'). Appending the clause after that last line puts a normative instruction immediately under a file list with no blank line, where a reader parses it as a continuation of the list rather than as a rule. §6 test 3 asserts offsets and order only, so it passes on the glued form. The review prompt's last Unit framing line is a sentence and hides the problem; the audit prompt is where the two commands stop being symmetric.
suggestion: Pin the leading separator as explicitly as the internal one: 'one blank line after the section's last existing line, then §2's clause, one blank line, then §3's clause, and a trailing newline'. Add the blank-line separators to test 3's offset assertions so a glued emission fails, and state which of the two commands' Unit framing sections the offsets are measured on - both, since their last lines have different shapes.

finding: A role name valid for the other phase falls between the spec's two definitions and gets no rule. Bullet 3 covers 'a name that is in the corpus but *inactive* for this spec — the per-spec deactivation of v0.32.0, reported in `skipped_roles`', while test 9 restates it as 'exists in the corpus but is in `skipped_roles` for this spec'. The corpus has two halves (`.tp/reviewers/`, `.tp/auditors/`), so `tp review --role go-safety` names something that is in the corpus, is not active for the review phase, and is not in review's `skipped_roles` either — it matches bullet 3's wording and fails test 9's. The implementer must decide whether it is 'unknown' (bullet 2's hint) or 'skipped' (bullet 3's hint), and the two hints are required to differ by test 9, so the choice is observable.
suggestion: Scope 'the corpus' to the phase in bullet 3 — 'in this phase's corpus but not active for this spec' — and add one sentence for the cross-phase name, which is a third operator mistake with its own hint ('go-safety is an audit role; use tp audit --role go-safety'). Add it to test 9 as a third case.

finding: §4.1 gives two definitions of the match set and they diverge in exactly the modes the same section legalises. Bullet 2 says <name> is matched against "the active role set for that phase — the same set the unrestricted invocation would emit"; bullet 3 contrasts a name "in the corpus but inactive". Verified on the shipped binary: `tp review <spec> --verify --findings <f>` emits one prompt whose role is "verifier" and `tp review <spec> --perspective regression` one whose role is "regression"; neither name is in the role corpus, and no corpus role is emitted in either mode. Under bullet 2's definition --role verifier --verify is legal and --role tester --verify exits 2; under bullet 3's corpus framing the reverse reads as intended. §6 does not settle it, because test 11 never names the role it passes.
suggestion: Define the match set once and explicitly as the set of role values the same invocation would emit without --role, and state the consequence: in --perspective and --verify modes that set is the single synthetic role, so corpus role names are refused there with exit 2. Then have test 11 assert both directions against that definition.

finding: §4.1 pins the match as "the single entry whose role equals <name>" and leaves the flag's own edge cases undecided; one of them is unavoidable in implementation. --role's zero value is the empty string, so "flag absent" and "--role \"\"" are indistinguishable to the command unless the spec says which behaviour wins — emit the whole panel, or exit 2 as an unknown role. The spec also does not say whether the match is case-sensitive or whitespace-trimmed (role ids in this corpus are lower-case kebab, so --role Tester and --role ax-economist<space> are plausible operator inputs), nor what a repeated --role a --role b does. Each is a pass/fail question a test must answer and none can be answered from the text.
suggestion: Add to §4.1: the match is exact and case-sensitive on the byte value; --role with an empty value is an unknown role and exits 2, not an absent flag; a repeated --role is refused with exit 2 (or last-wins — state which). Add one test for the empty value, since that is the case the implementation cannot avoid deciding.

finding: P2 (Batch Parity: what is easy for 1 must be equally easy for N) is not addressed, and §4's own evidence is the N case. §4's measured shortfall is operator-side - 'both cycles piped the JSON into a script and split it by role, every round' - i.e. one invocation producing all N prompts. §4.2 claims --role fixes that path too: 'For a human orchestrator it replaces the split script with one invocation per role.' That is N invocations replacing one, each of which re-parses the spec, re-reads review state, and re-emits every other top-level key (test 7 requires them byte-identical, so structured_elements, review_loop and skipped_roles are paid N times). §4.1's singular `--role <name>` and test 6's 'emits exactly one prompts[] entry' both foreclose a repeatable form, and the spec never says whether --role may be given more than once. The mechanism is a clear P1 win for the tp run path, where each unit genuinely wants exactly one prompt, and an unexamined P2 regression on the path the measurement came from.
suggestion: Say what --role does when repeated. Either declare it repeatable - `--role a --role b` emits the named subset, one invocation, prompts[] filtered to those entries, which serves both paths and keeps P2 - and amend test 6 to assert the subset rather than 'exactly one'; or declare it single-valued on purpose and say in §4.2 that the human orchestrator keeps the single unrestricted invocation, so the flag is not sold to a caller it makes worse.

finding: Test 10 requires that --role with each refusing mode "exits 2 with a hint naming both flags", but neither §4.1 nor §6 says the refusal is evaluated before the mode's own argument validation, and for most modes in the table it cannot be observed otherwise. --merge, --record, --resolve and --resolve-all each take a required file argument and already fail on their own when it is missing or unreadable (this repository records review_record.go exiting ExitFile for a missing --record file). A test written as a bare `tp review <spec> --merge --role tester` therefore observes a non-zero exit produced by the mode, not by the refusal, and the bare assertion "exits 2" does not separate the two causes.
suggestion: State in §4.1 that the --role refusal is checked during flag validation, before any mode's own preconditions. Have test 10 assert the exit code together with a required substring of the hint for each mode, and run each case with otherwise-valid mode arguments so a pass cannot be produced by the mode's own error path.

finding: Test 3 does not test §2.3's requirement. §2.3 places the clauses "after its last existing line" of ## Unit framing; test 3 asserts only that they fall "inside the ## Unit framing section, after the line naming the output file". Those are different positions. Verified on the shipped round-3 prompt: ## Unit framing continues for three more lines after the output-file line ("Produce findings for this round only…", "Loop budget: review round 3; 2 consecutive clean round(s) required, 0 so far.", "File reading: …"), so an implementation that inserts the clauses immediately after the output-file line passes test 3 while violating §2.3. "Inside the section" adds nothing either: ## Unit framing is the last section of the emitted prompt, so every byte after its heading is inside it.
suggestion: Assert the requirement rather than a weaker consequence of it: the clause block's start offset exceeds the end offset of the section's last pre-existing line, and the block is the tail of the prompt. Either name that last line per command, or assert it structurally — no byte of the pre-v0.36.0 prompt appears after the clause block.

finding: Test 9's only mechanical assertion is "The two hints differ", and no token of either hint is pinned anywhere. §4.1 says the unknown-role hint lists "the active roles" and the skipped-role hint "names it as skipped rather than unknown" — neither is a string a test can match. Any byte difference passes, including two hints that both read "unknown role: <name>" and differ only in the interpolated name, which is guaranteed to differ because the two cases necessarily pass different names. The test cannot fail on the defect it exists to catch.
suggestion: Pin a discriminating substring per hint: the skipped-role hint must contain a token such as "skipped" (or "deactivated for this spec") and the unknown-role hint must not contain it. Assert on those substrings instead of on inequality.

finding: §7's two sentences disagree about the gate's scope. Sentence 1 gates only the clauses: 'Nothing here ships until §2's and §3's clauses are replayed against the recorded rounds in spec/.tp-review/ and shown not to lose a finding tp used to surface.' Sentence 2 names the mechanism the gate is for: 'Every mechanism in this release hides, regroups or narrows what a reviewer sees - `--role` most of all'. So §4, identified in the same paragraph as the worst offender, is the one mechanism the gate does not cover. The scope cannot simply be widened either: the recorded rounds under spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/ are findings NDJSON, and --role's failure mode is a role's findings FILE never being produced because the orchestrator asked for the wrong name or looped over the wrong set - a shape recorded findings cannot exhibit, since every recorded row already came from a role that ran.
suggestion: Split the gate. Keep the replay for §2 and §3, whose risk is prompt text changing what a reviewer reports. For §4 name a different and executable gate: for a fixed spec and corpus, assert that the union of `tp review <spec> --role <r>` over every r in the emitted panel reproduces the unrestricted payload's prompts[] byte for byte, with no role omitted - that is the property whose violation loses a finding, and it is checkable without any recorded round.

finding: The flag's own surface is unspecified in three ways an implementer must decide before writing the cobra registration. §4.1 never says whether `--role` is a string or a repeatable slice (bullet 1's 'reduced to the single entry' implies single, but a repeated flag then silently takes the last value rather than being refused); whether matching is case-sensitive or normalised, which matters because role names come from user-authored corpus filenames; and what `--role ''` does — an empty value matches no role, so it lands in bullet 2's unknown-role path with an exit-2 hint that reads oddly. §6 tests none of the three.
suggestion: One bullet in §4.1: `--role` takes exactly one value, is matched case-sensitively against the role name as the corpus spells it, and a repeated or empty `--role` exits 2 with the same hint as an unknown name. Add the repeated-flag case to test 8.

finding: §4.1's 'Every other top-level key is unchanged', pinned by test 7 as byte-identical, guarantees that the flag whose purpose is to stop shipping bytes the caller will not read keeps shipping one it already has. Measured on this round: the non-prompt keys are 2,774 bytes of JSON (structured_elements 1,654, review_loop 1,058, spec/spec_path 126, skipped_roles 2). structured_elements is the tables-and-lists inventory, and the emitted role prompt already restates all 22 of its entries as its 'Check each of these specifically' checklist -- so under --role the payload is one prompt plus a key duplicated inside that prompt, ~8% of what remains. That is small in absolute terms and worth naming only because test 7 turns it into a contract that a later release cannot narrow without breaking a test.
suggestion: Keep the byte-identical rule for the keys that carry information the single prompt does not (skipped_roles, review_loop) and say explicitly that structured_elements is retained for compatibility rather than because a --role caller needs it -- or scope test 7 to 'no key is dropped or altered' so a future --compact interaction is not pre-forbidden by a byte comparison.

finding: The release's headline cost figure and the number test 5 asserts are different quantities, and neither is written where the other is. §1 says '375 bytes, 69 words, measured on the exact strings §2 and §3 fix'; the two strings measure 374 bytes (197 + 177) and 69 words, so 375 counts one separator. §2.3 mandates placement 'after its last existing line ... one blank line between them', which makes the actual delta 378 bytes or more depending on the leading separator. Test 5 asks for 'exactly the two clauses plus their separators -- asserted as a byte count' and gives no count. So one cost has three values and the test that is supposed to fail on a reword has no number to fail against.
suggestion: Put the separator-inclusive delta in §2.3 where placement is fixed, have §1 quote that same number, and have test 5 cite it rather than restate the derivation.
